What, exactly, about the drink is so distracting? The viral debate raises bigger questions about who defines ‘professionalism’

The great iced coffee debate of 2026 is the latest submission to the young-people-just-don’t-get-it discourse and, of course, it’s as polarizing as ever.

Recruiters say you shouldn’t bring iced coffee to interviews , while young people are (rightly) asking: what’s the big deal? It’s one of those conversations that makes me cringe, given just how eagerly it springs up from the generational divide plaguing mainstream culture. And as usual, gen Z are cast as the entitled morons who want to live life with no rules or responsibilities, all to the detriment of the millennials and gen X-ers who have to deal with them.

Iced-coffeegate blew up on social media after the president of a recruiting firm shared a TikTok saying the drink “looks a little too casual” to hiring managers. With thousands of outraged responses across TikTok and Twitter/X, I was stunned to see so many people up in arms about someone bringing a coffee to an interview. Per one of my favorite comments: “It’s an iced coffee, not a bomb!”

Still, these discussions are a reminder of the deep chasms that exist generationally and culturally when it comes to notions of professionalism and how we’re supposed to show up in public life. As I scrolled through endless posts lamenting how terrible youth culture is, I wondered seriously: what is it about an iced coffee that feels so distracting or unprofessional?

Then again, so much of this is tied up in the cultural symbolism and associations we create with the world around us. Iced coffee? So gen Z. But what if it was a warm coffee, in a nice, grown-up looking travel mug? Or what if it was just water? See how silly and arbitrary it all is?

But let’s put the iced coffee to the side.

The bigger picture is that for the most part, rules of professionalism are rooted in racist constructs. From Eurocentric dress and hair codes to the weaponization of “what’s appropriate to say at work” to suppress dissenting discourse and discourage non-conformity, “professionalism” is and has always been about social control. These unknowable norms are mostly code for whiteness, and are regularly and violently weaponized against racialized, disabled, poor, young or otherwise minoritized people.

Unfortunately, much of how we are able to show up in public overall is also guided by workplace rules – a clear sign of the death grip that capitalism has on us. Workplaces function as enforcement agents of white supremacy in the office, in ways that inevitably spill over into our lives outside it. As oppressive dress codes limit religious expression, and hair discrimination pushes Black women to alter their natural hair textures, the workplace has become the arbiter of how we are allowed to exist.

Even higher institutions are complicit in pushing the importance of professionalism. Just a few months ago, Tuskegee University, a historically Black institution, announced a new dress code prohibiting students from wearing bonnets and durags in class or any official campus spaces.

Their reasoning? Well, in an email to the student body, the Tuskegee president, Dr Mark Anthony Brown, said the new rules were intended to “prepare [students] with a solid foundation for the workforce.

“Employers are less forgiving and too often presentation may overrule stellar preparation,” he wrote.

We spend far too much time policing irrelevant things like iced coffees, while gen Z languishes in a punishing job market amid the steadily rising cost of living. And as long as we remain beholden to professionalism culture and its shackles, we’ll continue the generational culture wars while young people bear the cost.

items.lbText:
The country’s far-right president is courting billionaire investors by removing a block on foreign ownership of land and natural resources

O n 19 September, Marta Sahores, an 84-year-old chemistry professor and activist who has mobilised against mega-mining projects for more than two decades, took to the streets in Argentina . Alongside workers, retirees, students, Indigenous groups and human rights organisations, Sahores was there to protest against the country’s far-right president, Javier Milei. During the marcha de la bronca – the “march of anger” – protesters held signs reading, among other rallying cries, “The land is not for sale”.

Marching in Esquel, a town nestled in the foothills of the Andes in Chubut province, she also held up a sign defending the country’s water resources against what she called the government’s “handover” to investors.

“When foreigners buy land, they buy land with rivers and lakes. They take our water, they take our soil,” says Sahores. “We stand for real democracy and environmental sovereignty.”

Sahores and fellow activists are rallying to overturn Milei’s broad deregulation decree , especially the measures against land protections. “Fortunately, we are many, and we are fighters,” Sahores says. “We’re in the streets when we need to be, and we’re in the courts when we need to be.”

In Argentina, land rights have become a critical political issue. Foreigners own about 13m hectares (32m acres) of the country’s land – approximately 5% , an area roughly the size of England. Since Milei took office on December 2023, his campaign to open resource-rich areas to foreign investment and roll back the protections of the 2011 Land Law – which critics say is already undercut by its non-retroactive scope – has alarmed advocates who say it deepens extractivism, contributes to housing inequality and displaces Indigenous communities.

The 2011 Land Law caps how much rural land foreigners can own: no more than 15% of any single department – the subdivision below a province – and no more than 30% in the hands of a single nationality. Yet departments such as Lácar, in the Patagonian province of Neuquén, exceed both limits, explains Tomás Costa, a researcher with the Land Observatory at the University of Buenos Aires (UBA).

In Lácar, part of a region known for its glacial lakes and native forests, about 54% of land is foreign-owned. Of that, about 30% (144,313 hectares) is concentrated in a small number of US entities that own 14 times as much land as the Curruhuinca , a Mapuche community that has spent years demanding access to clean water .

Last week, the supreme court overturned a previous ruling that had blocked Milei’s attempts to repeal the Land Law, effectively clearing the path for the controversial reform to move forward just two months after a failed effort in Congress.

Amid mass protests, Milei’s party, La Libertad Avanza passed a stripped-down version of its inviolability of private property bill in the Senate this August, withdrawing its two most contentious provisions: one that would have raised the foreign land cap from 15% to 25%, and another that would fast-track land development after wildfires .

The approved bill, still pending in the chamber of deputies, also included articles to fast-track evictions and make it harder to expropriate lands for public works, favouring private interests.

The project is part of the libertarian president’s broader scheme to court foreign investors such as Peter Thiel, who recently acquired a 1% stake in Vista, an oil producer in Argentina’s main fossil fuel reserves, Vaca Muerta.

In 2024 , Milei enacted his large investment incentive regime, or Rigi , which relaxes limits on how much money investors can send back to their parent companies, lowers the corporate income tax rate and exempts imported machinery from tariffs, with 30 years of regulatory stability guaranteed.

A proposed “ super Rigi ” expands on the regime for “frontier mega-projects” such as AI datacentres and semiconductor manufacturing, which require massive quantities of water and critical minerals including lithium, of which Argentina has one of the largest reserves .

The impact of Milei’s agenda is being acutely felt by Indigenous communities threatened by eviction orders in land disputes that have dragged on for decades, says Pablo Volkind, professor at UBA’s School of Economic Sciences.

“It’s not ‘what could happen’; it’s what’s already happening,” Volkind says, noting that Milei’s deregulation push has ushered in “a flood of evictions” in Jujuy, Neuquén, Chubut and Misiones, emboldening courts to move faster on property cases that might have been contested in a different political climate.

Volkind heads the Land Observatory, which produced an interactive map of foreign land ownership in Argentina, letting users visualise how foreign holdings overlap with natural reserves, national parks, glaciers and Indigenous presence. Many of the lands exceeding the ownership cap sit along the Argentine cordillera, stretching from Salta and Jujuy in the north to Tierra del Fuego, rich in mining resources and freshwater reserves in glacial and periglacial zones.

In April, Milei signed a reform to the glacier law that authorises mining in previously protected regions.

Another area of high foreign ownership is the Paraná River basin, along Misiones, Corrientes and Entre Ríos, a key export corridor. In Puerto Libertad, Misiones, near the Iguazu Falls, the Chilean forestry company Arauco controls so much land that the mayor must ask it for permission before advancing public projects such as a 10-hectare industrial park .

The areas high in foreign landholdings are also among those with the largest Indigenous populations, for whom Milei’s advances are yet another chapter in what campaigners and experts consider a history of systemic racism and land dispossession.…

Charlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation Felix

H ow often does this happen? You open the fridge and find some ingredient you meant to use but didn’t get round to, and even though it’s still edible you think perhaps it’s just easier to throw it away. In the UK it’s estimated that an average household wastes about three meals a week , or 156 meals a year.

Household fridges are one thing. But across the food sector, more than 1bn meals’ worth of easily accessible surplus food is wasted each year in the UK for the same reason: because it is easier to throw it away. That equates to 470,000 tonnes – enough to feed every child in the UK three meals a day for a month. When so many people are struggling to afford food, that is a staggering amount – and what’s even more shocking is that it is good quality and nutritious.

We hear a lot about grocery stores and restaurants throwing out perfectly edible food, but they are just a small part of the problem. The vast majority of food waste , about 850m meals, comes from farms, followed by food manufacturing facilities with 178m meals, another 71m from the hospitality and food service sector, and finally 12m meals from the retail sector.

When I say easily accessible, I mean this is food we have the capacity to rescue and get to people. The organisation I head, Felix, is a food rescue charity. We recover edible surplus food that would otherwise go to waste and get it to more than 8,000 organisations that do amazing work to feed people in need. This food sustains lunch clubs for older people where friendships are forged and isolation is addressed. It supports food pantries, where families can access a weekly bag of shopping for just a few pounds. And it can provide meals in homelessness shelters and refuges. But with food insecurity rising, so too is the need for the food we recover. So we must rescue more of that billion-meal surplus.

In our food system, unavoidable surplus food is generated at every stage of the supply chain. On farms, unpredictable weather, grading standards and mismatches between harvest volumes and buyer orders contribute to the enormous quantities of edible produce without a home. But we are working with farmers to ensure this food is getting to people’s plates; almost half the food we gave out last year was fresh fruit and vegetables.

In manufacturing, production overruns, packaging changes and quality control measures create surplus that cannot be sold through normal channels. But there are bright spots – and an incredible example is the food manufacturer Premier Foods. When their noodle nests don’t pass quality control, we take them and use a partner organisation to repack and label them. We are doing a similar project with 2 Sisters Food Group, a huge manufacturing company that uses late-night surplus factory capacity to repack breaded chicken with minor visual defects.

We are also working with supermarkets such as Asda, Co-op, Ocado, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose. They give us a huge amount of stock that we get straight back out to every part of the UK.

So many companies are doing their bit, but the reason many are not is economics. It is cheaper for a business to waste food than to give it to people: the corporation tax system does not reward food donation in the same way it does a financial one. In addition, public subsidies for alternative disposal routes – such as turning food waste into animal food or biogas – provide profit. This creates a market that actively pulls surplus away from human consumption. We must change this.

That is why Felix has started the Redistribution Revolution. Felix, City Harvest, Community Shop, The Bread and Butter Thing, His Church, Feeding Britain, Neighbourly and the wider Felix and Xcess Networks have formed the Food Redistribution Partnership UK, working together to rescue more food. Backed by the government, we have launched a national programme to redistribute surplus food that aims to triple the amount of food we redistribute over the next decade. According to our research, about 1% of all excess food in the UK food system is redistributed by charities. France redistributes about twice that , while the US does three times more.

Our revolution needs food businesses to make redistribution the default route for all surplus food, and view it as an opportunity for social good. We need philanthropists to invest in the infrastructure required to store and move the food. And we need the government to change the tax system and make it more financially viable for companies to get food to people.

Finally, we need donations and volunteers to help us rescue and deliver more food.

We know surplus food is out there, and while it is very important to recognise that redistribution is not a systemic solution to poverty, we are certain that good food is going to waste. Rescuing it can be a powerful way to alleviate the symptoms of food insecurity, and to support organisations that are helping people tackle the challenges in their lives.

Charlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation Felix

Inhabitants of the Hebrides and Shetland tell of how fuel costs are putting the squeeze on commuting, services, food and more

A s fuel prices reach the highest level in the UK since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Scottish islanders are feeling the pain more than most. On the mainland, the price of diesel has soared to a record high of 200.01p a litre, bringing the cost of filling an average family car to more than £110, according to the RAC. Petrol has risen by a third since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, averaging 174.71p – increasing to 195.64p in motorway service areas.

In the Hebrides and Shetland, prices at the forecourt have jumped even higher, with some fuel stations selling diesel for more than 220p a litre during the initial rise.

While European governments appear to have staved off a US export ban that could have sent prices even higher, in Shetland the lack of competition and the cost of shipping to remote areas have made it the most expensive place in the UK for fuel. The ramifications for island life have been immediate.

Adam, 43, who lives in North Uist in the Outer Hebrides, said diesel had reached £2.28 a litre on the island, making his 45-mile round commute particularly expensive. He and his wife have diesel cars that they need for work and transporting their three children.

“You accept that things are more expensive, especially food because there’s more distance to travel and we are further from distribution centres. Same with getting things delivered here because you have to drive more miles. But when something like the price of diesel skyrockets, it really hammers people here more than other places around the country,’” he says.

In between work and dropping children off with his wife, Adam says they really rack up the miles. To cut costs, Adam says the family is having to buy the cheapest food they can, given that food prices are also dependent on the price of diesel that haulage companies pay.

“It’s come down a bit in the last week or so. I never thought I’d look up at a £2.18 diesel price and think: ‘Oh, quick, I better fill up now.’ It’s really bad. Although people think of this place as really tiny, you’re in your car all the time. I average 15,000 miles a year, and my wife does even more because she’s a health visitor. She gets the same mileage as someone who’s a health visitor in the central belt, yet we pay a lot more,” he says.

About 26,000 people live in the Outer Hebrides, mainly on the largest islands of Lewis and Harris. Adam says rising prices have also hit accessibility to public services, which are already difficult to reach for islanders.

“The Scottish government say they want to help repopulate places like this but in reality, they are not offering much practical support. For example, my daughter had a referral to a paediatrician for a hearing test so I had to take her to Stornoway for that. It involved booking ferries, driving more than 100 miles and staying in a hotel. We can claim some money back from the patient travel scheme but they only offer you £40-£50 for a hotel. Because of the costs getting there, the NHS stops being free at the point of use because we can’t be treated locally,” he says.

Bob, a postman who lives in Shetland, said that people in the North Sea archipelago were frustrated by rising fuel prices while also being a hub for the oil and gas industry.

“You are resigned to it. It’s always been slightly more expensive than everywhere else, so you have to pay the prices. What can you do? Fuel poverty has always been an issue up here. It’s ironic in a sense given we are near where a lot of the oil and gas arrives from the North Sea. Yet, we are paying higher prices than anyone else. It’s the same with the windfarms,” he says.

Bob says that islanders often have no other choice but to drive, especially when getting to work.

“Most jobs are in Lerwick so unless you live in town, you need to drive. There is a bus service but people who work don’t use it much because it’s difficult to make their hours,” he says. “I only ever drive small cars. I have a Fiat 500 so it’s not too bad. But an awful lot of people have big 4x4s up here because of the weather. Diesel prices will be having a big impact on them.”

Ryan, 25, from the Isle of Benbecula in the Outer Hebrides, says the soaring costs mean many islanders are having to cut back.

“A lot of family and friends up here are taking fewer journeys than they would normally outside work. For a lot of people, it’s a case of just going to work and going to the shops. Even those journeys are not short. The Western Isles span 130 miles. South Uist itself is about an hour top to bottom. A lot of us easily get through a few tanks a month on fuel. It’s a lot of the money that’s getting spent up here,” he says.

Ryan works in a nearby hotel and is paid close to the minimum wage. With almost no public transport, he says he needs to drive to work because of how rural it is. The cost of his commute has meant sacrificing some of the things he likes to do with his girlfriend.

“Me and my girlfriend like to go to restaurants that are a bit of a distance away, around half an hour drive. We’ve not done that in a while. I think it’s safe to say that the cost of fuel will be affecting businesses because they’ll be getting fewer customers,” he says.

As fuel costs rise, islanders have started taking jerry cans to the mainland to stock up on cheaper fuel, even to just save a few pennies a litre, Ryan says. Normally, the cans are used in the winter to stock up when high winds and choppy seas disrupt deliveries to the islands and pumps run dry.…

items.title: Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess | Gaby Hinsliff
items.author: Gaby Hinsliff
items.content:
Badenoch would never have reopened the door on Brexit, but now that the PM has, it suits the Conservatives to let him walk through it

There’s no way on earth it should have worked, but somehow he may have got away with it. Last week, the actor Richard E Grant became the first contestant on The Traitors – a show whose only unbreakable rule is never to let anyone know you’re the murderer – to gleefully announce within minutes of being selected that yes, haha, Yet even then many of his fellow contestants seemed to like him too much to recoil.

And that, roughly speaking, is now Andy Burnham’s Brexit strategy. After years of Labour politicians – not least Burnham himself, in the Makerfield byelection, without which he would not now be prime minister – trying to hide their real feelings about Brexit, Burnham has decided just to tell the truth and hope people roll with it. Leaving hasn’t worked, he said bluntly last week in Liverpool, and Britain should consider the alternatives. If you’re a leaver who suspects him of being out to unwind Brexit – well, yes, he is. This bold strategy seemingly surprised much of his own cabinet, an early lesson in how he likes to work for those who hadn’t studied his Manchester operation closely enough. But the oddly muted initial response to what would once have been a seismic shock suggests it’s wrongfooting some opponents, too.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

items.title: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
items.author: Morwenna Ferrier
items.content:
It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?

Temperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.”

I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues.

For all the howls of a ‘stitch-up’, it’s hard to see what ministers were supposed to do, as the alternatives risked worse outcomes

BT to buy broadband supplier TalkTalk in £400m rescue deal, saving 900 jobs

“A ll the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest,” thundered Virgin Media O2. It’s not an unreasonable view of BT’s hurried weekend acquisition of TalkTalk . Once upon a time, TalkTalk was seen as a plucky upstart performing the useful role of irritant to BT’s giant Openreach broadband operation. Now the challenger is being consumed by the dominant player via a pre-pack administration that minimises short-term political headaches.

Here’s the problem, though, with the cosy stitch-up thesis. For all the howls of outrage, it’s hard to see what the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, who gave her blessing by issuing a little-used public interest notice, was supposed to do differently. Alternative approaches, notably a chaotic collapse of TalkTalk without a rescue plan for the customers, risked worse outcomes.

OK, perhaps the worst fears of GP surgeries and hospitals being disconnected at a stroke, and thousands of vulnerable customers losing their internet connection, were overdone. But, in Nandy’s shoes, you probably wouldn’t take the risk. TalkTalk, after all, had had months to find a buyer but failed to land a credible deal even when its retail division and its wholesale unit, PXC, were up for grabs separately.

Disappointed would-be buyers blame the reluctance of BT, as the critical supplier to TalkTalk, to extend financial support to a new ownership vehicle. From BT’s point of view, however, one can see why another private equity backer for TalkTalk wouldn’t feel like an improvement on the last one . As it is, BT will be booking £100m as a non-payment of a debt even as it takes control.

The deep problem here is that TalkTalk – Sir Charles Dunstone’s creation more than 20 years ago – hasn’t been doing much real challenging work of late. After going through the refinancing wringer more times than is healthy, it was a financially distressed company. At the last count, borrowings were in the region of £1.5bn, a staggering sum for a loss-making business with only 1.5 million retail customers and 1 million wholesale ones. Telephony, remember, tends to be a low-margin game even when things are going well.

That is not to say the politicians get a free pass. Successive governments have been told many times by the regulator Ofcom that a “supplier of last resort” regime should be in place in the broadband market, just as it is in energy and water. The logic is simple: in extremis, there should be a way for a government-supported operation to step in to prevent sudden disconnections and look for an orderly permanent solution.

The unavoidable fact, though, is that such a regime didn’t exist with TalkTalk. That glaring hole in the regulatory setup needs to be addressed for future cases. But a weekend arrangement with BT , however objectionable in theory, at least has the advantage of not drawing on a penny of public money.

The medium-term regulatory test will be to ensure BT and Openreach can’t abuse the advantage of gobbling TalkTalk. There was a theatrical public exchange of letters between the BT chief executive, Allison Kirkby, and the Ofcom boss, Dame Melanie Dawes. The former pleaded for regulatory mercy, in effect, for removing a political problem; the latter replied that applying the regulatory framework was a statutory duty.

It’s anyone’s guess how that will work out in practice since the wriggle room would seem to be enormous. But the guiding principle hasn’t changed – wholesale operators need to have access to Openreach’s network on reasonable commercial terms. TalkTalk couldn’t make it pay but that, in the end, seems primarily to be a story of its own perilous financing. Wrapping the business into BT is very far from being ideal – but it’s not the worst pragmatic fudge.

items.lbText:
Banks and building societies raise prices as turmoil in bond markets increases expectations of base rate rise

The average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage has hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years, as jitters in the money markets make the loans more expensive for lenders to offer.

Figures from financial information provider Moneyfacts show the average is now 6.00%, its highest point since September 2023, while the average two-year fixed rate is not far behind at 5.98%, its highest since December of the same year.

In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put up prices as turmoil in global bond markets has increased expectations of a base rate rise .

Meanwhile, borrowers in Great Britain have seen their choice of fixed-rate mortgages costing below 5% shrivel to only nine options, according to Moneyfacts. That marks a 99% plunge in the market since the start of last month, when there were 1,494 deals priced below that level.

There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages .

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfacts, said the impact on rates had been “brutal”.

She said: “Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers. Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed.”

The rise in prices is bad news for borrowers finishing existing fixed-rate deals who at the start of the year may have been looking forward to falling costs, as well as those hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a property.

Figures from the HomeOwners Alliance show the monthly cost of a £250,000 loan fixed at 6% for five years is £158 higher than the same-sized loan locked in at 4.94%, which was the average rate reported by Moneyfacts at the start of February.

There are already signs that higher mortgage costs are weighing down the housing market, with Nationwide building society last week reporting that annual price growth had halved in September .

Ian Harris, the president of the estate agents’ body NAEA Propertymark, said members were “seeing first-hand how sensitive buyers are to mortgage rates”, and the rapid disappearance of sub-5% deals would add further pressure to affordability. He said: “For some buyers, even a relatively small increase in monthly repayments can mean they have to reduce their budget or step back from a purchase altogether. Equally, homeowners coming off fixed-rate deals may face significantly higher repayments, which could affect their decision to move.”

Sykes Holiday Cottages showed no empathy and insisted on paperwork we didn’t have so soon after my husband’s death

W e booked a break with Sykes Holiday Cottages for 11 of us to celebrate my mum’s 80th birthday last February. The cost was £2,400, paid for by my 87-year-old dad, but it was my husband who made the booking.

In January, my husband was diagnosed with aggressive lymphoma, and he died 10 days before the trip. My parents and some other members of the party still planned to take the holiday, and my dad informed Sykes of the death, since my husband was their point of contact.

Sykes declared that the booking could not be honoured in my late husband’s name and that they would need a copy of his death certificate to move it into my name. We did not have one since an inquest into the death had been ordered.

Sykes said a copy of my marriage certificate would suffice. I submitted this, only to be told that “an official document recognised by the state that confirms the passing of the deceased” was required.

We provided a screenshot of the inquest listing from the coroner’s court website but were advised that this was not sufficient evidence.

My GP wrote a letter confirming the death, but Sykes did not reply, and by then we were all too distressed to continue.

Later, Sykes sent numerous emails to my late husband’s email address asking whether he had enjoyed the stay. We never received a refund, and I have not felt emotionally strong enough to do anything further before now.

I could hardly believe what I was reading as I trawled through Sykes’s correspondence. Its response, on being informed of your husband’s untimely death, was to send him an email asking for information.

When Sykes received the requested marriage certificate, the company simultaneously stated in an email that this provided sufficient proof for the booking to be transferred to your name, and that the booking could not be transferred without an official confirmation of death.

The GP letter confirming the death merely elicited an email saying Sykes would be in touch. By then, the trip was two days away. Sykes still did not amend the booking name, nor did it acknowledge the link to the coroner’s inquest listing.

The next you heard from them was the first of several emails addressed to your late husband hoping that he had enjoyed the holiday. When you asked them to stop using his email address, Sykes apologised for the “inconvenience”.

Four days later, when you had to complain about another such email to him, you were told unapologetically that feedback forms are sent automatically. By then, Sykes had been informed multiple times over a fortnight that your husband had died.

Sykes, I discover, does not have an official bereavement policy which, given the size of the business, is poor enough. But empathy does not require an official mandate and you received none.

Its onerous name change requirements are more suitable for a visa application than checking into a Cumbrian cottage. It refunded the £2,400 pronto when I got in touch and added £150 in “goodwill”. I think that’s a paltry sum for the distress it caused, but you have accepted it so you can put the ordeal behind you.

A spokesperson said: “We have contacted the family directly to apologise and resolve the matter, and are reviewing our processes to ensure situations like this are always handled with the care and sensitivity they deserve.”

Our spirits need some good news, so here are some tales of how customer service ought to be.

“We bought a secondhand Scandibørn bed from a third-party seller and found four screws were missing,” writes CC . “They were so specialist that no shop even knew what they were called. We contacted Scandibørn with low expectations of help, but they immediately offered to send us the missing screws for free. Exemplary customer service, which has earned a customer for life.”

MS , meanwhile, raises his revamped hat to Tilley. “Thirty years ago I bought a Tilley hat, which became a constant companion on walks and holidays. It was beginning to show its age and, since the label promised a lifetime guarantee, I contacted Tilley. I was asked to submit photographs and was promptly invited to choose from three designs. The replacement was dispatched within days, with a handling charge of £20. Sadly, this one will outlast me.”

We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us at consumer.champions@theguardian.com or write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject to our terms and conditions .

A story of storico ribelle, produced by a small group of mountain herders according to a traditional farming system based on seasonal and rotational grazing

My journey into the world of storico ribelle began with a shared passion for photography and the mountains. A close friend of mine lives in the Orobie Alps . He loves the mountains and the natural environment that surrounds him, and we share the same passion for photography. When I finally went to visit him, I discovered a way of experiencing the mountains that was very different from the one I knew growing up in the Apennines, where I come from.

What struck me was not only the landscape, but the relationship people still have with it. Here, I discovered a world where the mountain is not simply a place to visit or explore, but a place to live and work. A world where cheese is still a tradition rather than an industrial product, and where the rhythms of the seasons, the animals and the daily work of the alpeggiatori – the mountain herders – are still deeply connected.

There was a poetry in this way of life that immediately inspired me. Waking before sunrise, milking, making cheese, moving with the animals and working until darkness: there was almost no separation between life and work.

I felt compelled to photograph this world. I wanted to tell the story of people who continue to choose a demanding way of life in a time when agriculture is increasingly industrialised and traditional knowledge is disappearing.

In the Orobie Alps, cheese is inseparable from the landscape that gives it life. Steep pastures, stone shelters and seasonal migration have shaped a rural culture for centuries. Animals move with the seasons, milk follows them, and cheese becomes a way of preserving a way of life.

Storico ribelle was born from this tradition – and from a decision to defend it. For generations, bitto cheese was made in small Alpine dairies and exchanged locally for essentials such as grain and salt. During summer, herders moved their animals progressively higher, following the pastures. Along the routes, calecc – simple stone shelters – were used for milking and transforming fresh milk into cheese. The wheels were taken to mountain cellars, or casère , where they could mature for years.

In 1996, the introduction of the bitto DOP (protected designation of origin) brought new regulations. Some producers considered the requirements incompatible with the traditional Alpine system they wanted to preserve. They chose to continue making cheese according to their own methods, outside the DOP. Eventually, a new name emerged: storico ribelle, or historic rebel.

The name reflects resistance, but the deeper story is one of continuity: preserving a relationship between livestock, pasture, milk, cheese and mountain life. That relationship can still be found across Val Gerola, Valtellina and Val Brembana.

At Alpe Pedena, Oreste Pedrelli, 56, has spent the last 10 years herding. He has been making cheese since he was eight, learning the craft from his grandparents. At Alpe Ancogno Soliva, Carlo Duca works with his brother Luigi. Their cheese is renowned for its extraordinary ageing potential, with some wheels maturing for up to 10 years.

At about 2,000 metres, Trona Vaga is the highest storico ribelle Alpine pasture. Manuele, born in 1988, runs the pasture with his partner, Erica, who came to cheesemaking from a completely different background. She studied languages and taught herself the craft as an adult.

Their stories reveal that tradition can be inherited, but it can also be chosen. This is particularly important among a younger generation. Michele Sassella, 15, continues the practice with his mother and sister in memory of his father, Alfio, who dedicated his life to protecting mountain breeds, natural farming rhythms and Alpine biodiversity.

Davide Peregalli, 16, has spent his summers at Alpe Vesenda since he was eight. Gioele Pedercini, 17, has already completed three summer seasons as an Alpine herder while studying agriculture. Valentina, 20, brings another perspective: with a degree in agricultural studies, she is the young cheesemaker at Alpe Orta Soliva.

They represent a generation that is not simply inheriting tradition, but deciding whether it has a future.

That future is fragile. Climate change is already affecting the tradition: scarce rain, increasingly violent storms, and pastures turning yellow even at high altitude. At the same time, increasingly demanding regulations make small-scale cheesemaking more expensive and labour-intensive. Yet the work continues.

Quality here comes with an extraordinary human cost. It means waking before sunrise, working throughout the day and going to bed after sunset. Every hour follows the animals. Milking, often by hand, is followed by transforming fresh milk into cheese. There is little distinction between work and life.

Storico ribelle represents more than a product. It is the result of pasture, animals, knowledge and time – and of people willing to resist the disappearance of a world.

The rebellion began with a choice not to follow a prescribed system. Today, its future depends on another choice: whether a new generation will continue to climb the mountain, care for the animals, make the cheese – and keep alive a way of life that exists almost nowhere else.

Cost of living crisis and drop in international students hits market for purpose-built accommodation

“I t was dead in the middle of summer, it was a shock,” says Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan. The fourth-year game design student at Abertay University was at home with her family thousands of miles away in Thailand when she discovered the owner of her Scottish studio flat had abruptly gone bust.

“I was like, my hands are tied. I’m not in the country. I don’t know what to do,” she says. Sriwiboonrattan was forced to act quickly to secure new housing for the academic year, which has just begun, paying £850 to have her possessions moved.

Her sudden upheaval was emblematic of the wider crisis in student housing. While UK universities face a financial crisis , providers of accommodation are grappling with falling international student numbers , a cost of living squeeze and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties.

A string of tower blocks known as purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA), targeted at more affluent students, have run into financial difficulty.

It had been touted as the ultimate student living: smart city centre blocks with gyms, cinemas and rooftop terraces have sprung up across the UK. A world away from the traditional image of dirty and dingy shared digs , the flats have offered a spacious alternative for their relatively affluent residents – often international students. Now, some sit half empty, and several schemes have gone bust .

Sriwiboonrattan was among nearly 70 students in Dundee who were left scrambling to find accommodation in late July after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a 116-room city centre block that had a concierge and a shared games lounge with a pool table.

Despite the boom in housing developed by financial institutions in recent years, many students heading off to university this term faced a different dilemma. Rents at the tower blocks have grown much faster than maintenance loans for British students, leaving PSBAs financially out of reach.

Meanwhile, the cost of living crisis has put financial pressure on students seeking university-owned or managed accommodation, while rising rents have hit those wanting to live in shared private rentals. Underlining the scale of the shortage of affordable housing, the students’ union in Bristol included an emergency support number for the housing charity Shelter in an email to new students.

At PSBAs, the national average rent, excluding London, is £191 a week including bills, according to the website StuRents.

At the top end, en suite rooms in Manchester command a weekly rent of £170 to £320 , whereas in London, en suite rooms are £250 to £650 a week , and studio apartments in Bloomsbury cost between £550 and £800 plus.

“I wasn’t able to get into PBSA because it is very expensive in Birmingham,” says Soham Chougale, 23, a student at University College Birmingham. “I am an international student, so my working hours are capped at 20 hours [a week in term time], which means I can’t afford to live in PBSA,” says Chougale, the education officer at UCB Guild of Students .

He lived in university-owned dorms for the first two years of his aviation management degree and now shares a two-bedroom privately rented flat with a friend. On campus, he paid £660 rent including bills a month during the first year, which rose by 10% in his second year; now he pays £700 rent a month, excluding bills.

While living on campus “gave me the best feeling of community” and “I still have those friends that I met on the first day”, the wifi was patchy, some facilities were broken and there was a mouse infestation, he recounts.

“PBSA can be quite pricey,” says Matthew Pointon, a real estate analyst at Capital Economics, but adds: “Normally professionally managed buildings are better in terms of quality.”

In London, which attracts the richest students, there is still demand for upmarket accommodation, but outside the capital, there is an oversupply in some cities, such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham.

This week, university staff began strikes in Dundee, Edinburgh and Nottingham over budget cuts, with the industrial action threatening to wipe out a term of teaching for many students.

In Nottingham, demand has fallen from a pandemic peak of 46,295 beds in 2022-23 to 42,290 beds in 2025-26, while 7,700 more PSBA beds came on to the market, the student housing charity Unipol calculated.

The number of students arriving from China has stagnated, and those from the new growth countries India, Pakistan and Nigeria are much more cost-conscious than the pre-Covid students from China , says Martin Blakey, an adviser on student living and the former chief executive of Unipol.

Deniz Yalçın, the chair of the Newington-Meadows branch of the Living Rent union in Edinburgh, says: “In Edinburgh, we’re seeing an explosion of PBSA despite the fact that this type of development is not needed and actually fuels the housing affordability crisis here.

“Many of them lie empty during most of the year, using the Fringe [festival] to bolster profits. Some have even been bought by the council to become temporary housing.”

Richard Ward, the head of research at StuRents, says the key issue is the big gap between maintenance loans and rents, after double-digit rental growth at PBSA blocks and shared houses in recent years.

Maintenance loans have declined in real terms because of below-inflation increases and frozen parental income thresholds. “And what have we seen? More students commuting ,” Ward says. “Outside of London, you’re talking about £300 rent a week to make a new PBSA scheme viable. Well, your average British student is paying about £160 a week.”

Occupancy rates at the tower blocks range between 71.3% in Glasgow, 69.9% in Coventry, 89.7% in Bristol and 95.3% in Exeter, as of August, according to StuRents.…

items.author: Rupert Jones
items.content:
Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and family

Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and family

The total amount stolen by criminals who hack into people’s emails and social media accounts and then pretend to be them has risen by more than 400% in a year, official UK data shows.

In many cases, the scammers are hijacking people’s accounts in order to use their identity to sell fake event tickets – such as to sold-out gigs – to unsuspecting friends and family.

The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25, according to the Report Fraud service run by the City of London police, which holds national responsibility for economic crime.

However, the true total may be much higher as many scam victims do not report the crime, often because they feel embarrassed, and sometimes because the individual amount of money involved was relatively small.

The Guardian previously featured the case of a music fan whose Instagram account was targeted by hackers, who used her identity to advertise tickets to an Oasis gig and stole £1,400 from her friends. She said the hackers impersonated her so well that her friends and family genuinely thought they were speaking to her.

Others have been scammed by fraudulent WhatsApp and text messages in which a criminal pretends to be their child or a relative who is in an emergency situation and urgently needs cash. This has been dubbed the “Hi mum” scam .

Data from Santander has shown that among customers of the bank, fraudsters pretending to be someone’s son were the most successful at extracting cash, followed by daughters.

Ch Supt Amanda Wolf, head of Report Fraud operations, said: “For most people, being hacked isn’t just a cyber issue – it’s personal. It can leave victims locked out of important accounts, worried about what information has been accessed, and concerned that criminals may use their identity to target others.”

She added that what starts with one compromised account “can quickly impact family, friends and colleagues as fraudsters exploit trusted relationships to commit further fraud”.

Report Fraud is launching an awareness campaign urging the public to protect their online accounts from hackers by switching to passkeys where they are available. A passkey uses an individual’s device and biometrics to authenticate them and cannot be hacked like a password.

items.lbText:
Cases of abuse, spitting, head-butting and sexual harassment, have spiked as transport police numbers have dwindled

When a train was halted outside Exeter St Davids station on Monday, rail staff leapt to one conclusion: there had been a violent incident on board.

“Someone will have kicked off,” one staff member said. “It happens all the time. My boss got head-butted recently.”

On this occasion, they were wrong – but their assumption told a tale. Figures released late last month showed the number of reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways had risen by a fifth, to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year.

Staff in particular have felt increasingly under threat. While the total numbers reported by the Office of Rail and Road in 2025-26 covered threats, verbal abuse, and contact that might not have resulted in any injury, they included nearly 2,500 physical assaults on workers – an average of about seven every day.

Their unions said the numbers were horrendous, but unsurprising: the RMT and TSSA unions have campaigned for more staffed stations and policing, after the number of British Transport Police (BTP) officers fell by more than 10% between 2024 and 2026.

Many rail staff wear body cams to record and log incidents of violence. “I think it’s so sad that we have those,” said Dave*, a rail worker in south-west England . However, after 20 years in the job, he said: “The threats, the abuse, the violence we see is off the scale.”

Drink and drugs play a part, he added. “We’re also seeing a lot more people with mental health issues. If you’re out on the street you can steer clear, but if you’re on a train or a platform you can’t. Our workplaces are becoming more and more dangerous.”

Steve, a guard based in the north of England, was punched in the head by a passenger: “It was my last train of the night. I’ve had to look away to see the door controls and the next thing I know, I’m waking up on the platform.”

Every guard gets verbally abused on a daily basis, he said, with behaviour worsening since the pandemic: “Now it’s mostly bad days, and you’re searching for good days, where nothing’s said, or nothing happens. The amount of times we’re getting threatened now with physical attacks, even when you walk through the train and say, ‘Tickets, please.’”

Even those working on the infrastructure can be on the receiving end. One rail contractor, Liam, based in Somerset, said: “We’re there working on the tracks and we sometimes get sworn at and even spat at. It’s just a minority, but somehow they think we’re responsible for slow journey times, cancelled trains. We’re in bright orange so we’re easy targets.”

The railway is by no means unique: bus drivers have faced repeated abuse and threats, as the Unite union has highlighted. Transport for London staff working on roads are issued with “spit kits”, or forensic saliva collection tubes, so common is that form of assault.

Violence against women and girls is of particular concern; at the Labour conference this week, the minister for buses and local transport, Simon Lightwood, described it as a “national emergency”.

Speaking alongside him, the mayor for the north-east, Kim McGuinness, said that as well as measures such as more staffing, lighting and CCTV, a crucial point for women was “knowing that if you raise an alarm something is going to be done. It’s a choice to use public transport or not … if you’re accepting 50% of the population don’t feel safe, that’s not good.”

The rail industry and police say some of the sharp rise in recorded assaults on passengers – up 36% last year – is due to greater reporting, including using discreet text messaging to the BTP.

But while many more incidents are now reported, plenty are not.

Emily, 24, was travelling home on a late-night train between Glasgow and Edinburgh last year when a stranger made a beeline for her. “He immediately tried to start a conversation and wouldn’t give up even when I showed no interest. He was asking what I’d been up to, whether I had a boyfriend, complimenting my outfit, and then it escalated really quickly.”

The man began rubbing Emily’s upper thigh and asking her intrusive questions about her sex life. “I froze and didn’t know what to do. I looked around but everyone else was oblivious. I tried to move but I was on the inside seat and he just grabbed my leg harder and leaned in towards me,” she said.

She managed to manoeuvre out of the seat and away from the man, who “shouted aggressively and called [her] a bitch”. Other passengers looked round but did not intervene. She moved to another carriage and arrived home shaken but decided not to report the incident.

“I wanted to just move on,” Emily said. “But I never used to think twice about getting on a train by myself at night and now I’m much more nervous.”

Edward, a trans man, was travelling home to Staffordshire with his partner, a trans woman, after a weekend in Wales . On a packed train from Aberystwyth, a man began loudly making homophobic comments and became confrontational.

“Normally in that situation I just walk on, but I physically couldn’t, we were so crammed,” Edward said. He finally yelled back, repeating: “You’re shouting homophobic abuse in front of your children.”

A railway worker eventually intervened and told the assailant and his family to move to another carriage. Edward chose not to report the incident to police, dissatisfied with the response to previous incidents. He now tries to avoid public transport: “I felt tearful, angry and scared afterwards.”

A fraction of passenger reports end up with arrest or prosecution. Last year, Sam was travelling north from London on a train packed with football supporters. As she tried to reach her reserved seat, a drunken man confronted her and pushed her backward.…

items.lbText:
Scammers reuse personal details harvested from fake Esta websites – and texts and calls can keep arriving for months

W hen the British actor Lisa Riley was preparing to travel to the US last year, she applied online for an Esta so she would not need a visa. After finding the site through a Google search she filled in her passport, bank and personal details and waited for the confirmation, which normally takes just under an hour.

When it failed to arrive, she emailed an address from the site where she had paid and got back a message unlike any she had seen before, with a link to a website that displayed a jumble of words and letters.

It was then she realised she had been scammed. But that was just the start of her problems, which persist to this day. She has been repeatedly targeted by criminals, receiving text messages and calls many times every week.

Riley was the victim of a fraud where criminals create websites similar to the legitimate one run by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). After fooling unsuspecting applicants they pocket a fee and use the personal details of victims for later scams.

Riley lost £16 – the cost of an Esta back then – but says there has been a huge increase in the number of scam calls and texts she has received in the 17 months since the fraud happened.

Often the person claims to be from her bank with queries about a money transfer. “Calls are once a week, easy – sometimes twice a week,” she says. “And the texts even more often.”

Research from Nationwide building society suggests that 15% of people have given personal information to something who later turned out not to be genuine, leaving them open to future frauds.

“Criminals do sadly retarget people after an initial scam,” says Annya Burskys, head of fraud operations at Nationwide. “They take the personal information they have gained and either sell it on to other scammers or use them to make follow-up bank impersonation calls , texts and emails appear more convincing.”

The fake Esta site that stole Riley’s personal details looked very similar to the official one and showed up high in search results, she says.

“The webpage was absolutely identical so there was nothing that would remotely make me fearful up until [I realised],” she says.

Criminals can use AI to recreate legitimate government sites and will frequently use key words such as “Esta”, in the domain name to try to portray legitimacy.

A spokesperson for the US CBP says some sites may demand action by the applicant quickly, a common tactic by criminals to try to get people to act without thinking something through.

Only use the official Esta website, which has a .gov address, or the mobile app.

“Applicants should protect their Esta confirmation number and payment details, retain application records, and review financial statements for unauthorised charges,” says the CBP spokesperson.

“Suspected fraud should be documented and reported promptly to the applicant’s financial institution and appropriate local government reporting channels.”

In the UK that means telling your bank and Report Fraud .

If you have inadvertently handed over your personal details you are at risk of future scams, so be alert to unexpected calls, texts or emails, says Burskys.

“Don’t feel pressured to act. A genuine call or message from your bank will never ask you to move money, never ask you to share codes, and will never tell you what to say to your bank or friends, family,” she says.

“Take a moment to verify who you’re speaking to and contact your bank directly using trusted contact information from your bank card or search for the official website if you’re unsure.”
